title: Scope, Boundaries, and Professional Judgement
introduction: The most technically capable security professional in the world can cause serious legal and professional harm by working outside their agreed scope. Scope is not bureaucracy. It is the legal boundary that separates authorised security testing from computer crime. Understanding scope — and the professional judgements that arise at its edges — is as important as any technical skill.

sections.heading: What scope actually means
sections.content:
Scope is the written agreement between the testing team and the client that defines exactly what is and is not authorised. It is a legal document. The written authorisation it provides is what makes penetration testing legal — the same actions performed without a scope agreement constitute unauthorised computer access in most jurisdictions.

Scope is defined in several ways:

**Domain scope**: specific domains (e.g., meridian-financial.com and all subdomains). Everything else — including domains that look related or that the client owns but did not list — is out of scope.

**IP scope**: specific IP addresses or ranges (e.g., 45.77.180.0/24). IPs outside this range are out of scope even if they appear related to the target.

**Application scope**: specific web applications by URL. Sometimes the main website is in scope but a third-party portal (Salesforce, Zendesk, HubSpot) is explicitly excluded.

**Technique scope**: what types of testing are authorised. Passive OSINT is almost always in scope. Active scanning, exploitation, and social engineering require explicit authorisation in the RoE.

Professional practice: before performing any action during an engagement, ask — is this asset listed in the scope? Is this action type authorised in the RoE? If either answer is uncertain, stop and confirm with the client before proceeding.

callout.title: Scope is not flexible
callout.content: A common error: a tester finds a related domain (a subsidiary, a sister company, an acquisition that shares infrastructure) and begins investigating it because 'it is clearly part of the same organisation.' This is out of scope. The scope document lists meridian-financial.com. It does not list meridian-advisory.com — even if they share the same owner, the same infrastructure, and are clearly related. Investigating meridian-advisory.com without written authorisation is a scope violation. Always get written amendment to scope before expanding investigation to assets not explicitly listed.

sections.heading: Four professional judgement scenarios
sections.content:
Scope creates clear cases (in scope or not in scope), but experienced testers regularly encounter situations that require professional judgement. Four of the most common:

**Scenario 1: Critical finding outside scope.**
During passive recon you discover that a domain closely related to the target (but not listed in scope) has an open database exposed to the internet — containing what appears to be the client's customer data. The domain is clearly operated by the same organisation.

Professional response: Do not investigate the out-of-scope asset further. Document what you observed and how (what query, what result). Contact the client immediately — verbally and in writing — to report what you found and ask whether they wish to expand the scope to include that domain. Do not wait for the final report. If the client confirms it is their infrastructure and grants verbal authorisation, get written confirmation before proceeding.

**Scenario 2: Finding that suggests an active breach.**
During passive recon you find a recent paste on Pastebin containing what appear to be current credentials for the target's Salesforce instance — posted three days ago, with a comment from the poster suggesting they have active access.

Professional response: This is not a testing finding. This is an active security incident that predates the engagement. Contact the client's emergency security contact immediately — not the project manager, but the person named in the RoE for emergency escalation. Screenshot the Pastebin page before reporting it, in case it is removed. This overrides the engagement timeline — it is reported now, not at report-out.

**Scenario 3: Scope lists a domain that resolves to a shared hosting provider.**
The scope lists client.com. Your investigation reveals client.com resolves to a shared hosting IP address — the same IP serves dozens of unrelated websites. Active scanning that IP would potentially affect non-client systems.

Professional response: Flag this to the client before active scanning begins. Shared hosting is a common situation where IP-scope testing needs to be handled carefully. Get written clarification from the client confirming that the shared IP is accepted, or that testing should be restricted to the application layer (not the IP) to avoid affecting co-hosted sites.

**Scenario 4: In-scope system shows signs of prior compromise.**
During active testing (not passive recon, but applicable to understand), you find a webshell left by a previous attacker on an in-scope server.

Professional response: Stop testing that system immediately. Document what you found — the URL of the webshell, the access it provides, a screenshot of its interface (without executing any commands). Report to the client emergency contact. This is an incident, not a finding. The client needs to know that a real attacker may have active access to this server before you continue.

callout.title: Immediate escalation vs final report
callout.content:
Two categories of findings require immediate escalation — not waiting for the final report:

1. Any finding suggesting active compromise by a real attacker (not the testing team)
2. Any finding so critical that the client needs to act before active testing continues — e.g., credentials actively in use, live data exposed publicly, active phishing infrastructure targeting the client's customers

Everything else goes in the final report. Professional judgment about which category a finding falls into is one of the skills that experience develops. When in doubt, escalate — a phone call that turns out to be unnecessary is far better than a delayed report of an active breach.

sections.heading: When does passive reconnaissance end?
sections.content:
This is a question beginners rarely ask and experienced professionals answer clearly: passive reconnaissance ends when the attack surface map is complete — not when you have exhausted every possible query.

Criteria for passive recon completion:

**Asset coverage complete**: every in-scope domain has had WHOIS, all DNS records, subdomain enumeration, and search engine reconnaissance performed. Every discovered subdomain has been processed through the same sequence.

**Diminishing returns**: the last two hours of passive recon produced no new findings that were not already covered by existing categories in the attack surface map. New queries are confirming what is already known rather than adding new intelligence.

**Attack surface map is populated at all four tiers**: there are findings at Critical, High, Medium, and Low levels. The map tells you where to start active testing and what to prioritise.

**Documentation is complete**: every finding has a source, evidence, severity, and recommended action. The reconnaissance report section can be written from the documentation without going back to re-run any queries.

There is no such thing as 'finished' in information gathering — there is always one more query to run. The professional discipline is knowing when the map is actionable, not when it is theoretically complete.

callout.title: The diminishing returns test
callout.content: After two consecutive hours of passive recon with no new findings that do not fit existing categories, passive recon is almost certainly at diminishing returns. That is the practical signal that the attack surface is mapped. The last few hours of passive recon often produce the most interesting edge-case findings — which is why the two-hour rule is two hours, not thirty minutes. But it is also why extending indefinitely produces noise rather than intelligence.

keyTerms.definition: The specific conditions governing an engagement: authorised hours, notification requirements, emergency contacts, technique authorisations, and stop conditions. Read completely before any action.
Any action performed against assets or using techniques not explicitly authorised in the scope document. A scope violation may constitute computer crime regardless of intent.

Reporting a finding to the client during the engagement rather than waiting for the final report. Required for findings suggesting active breach or findings so critical the client must act immediately.

The point in passive reconnaissance where continued querying confirms existing findings rather than producing new intelligence. The practical signal that the attack surface map is complete enough to proceed.
